title: The London show, the dog-band reviews and the Dixie Club
summary: He describes critics' mockery, the troops' response, the Dixie Club contract and his return to New York in 1920.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Go right ahead. You played the show.

We played the show. Before we played the show, we rehearsed in the show. When all the Englishmen laughed at us, the papers carried reports that we was a dog band. Some of them said we was yelping hounds. And they didn't describe our music with anything but was no good. That's the critics in London. And you have a picture that was taken backstage. And all the people sitting down are reporters. That afternoon on the 5th, we opened in the show. We got a fair hand for when the doughboys from the United States Army heard we were in town because we had entertained every one of them that passed through New York. They roughed that show. They crowded the show. That night when we played our numbers, it looked like the roof fell in. George Ruby, who was the head man of the show, along with Albert DeCobble's wife, she was the lead woman in the show, he gave Mr. DeCobble an ultimatum. He says, You take them out the show or I don't go on. Mr. DeCobble had to go out and buy a club to put us in. In the meantime, we worked two weeks in the Palladium. We worked one week up in the north of England. And we came back and opened the 6 and 8 Bond Street Club. We used to name the lady change the Dixie Club. For that contract you have there, we made $200 a week. And 80 pounds extra for every place we played. Extra than the place we were supposed to be. We were cleaning up almost $2,000. That was worth $480, $82, or $83. We stayed there. We finished the contract with him. And they had a clause. If he stayed in there, he didn't have to pay our fair back. In the meantime, I signed the contract with Mitchell and Booker. Rectors at Tottenham Court Road. Now we have, in this band, Robinson, Stillworth, Shields, Bara, Christian, and myself. We go and open that Rectors, on Tottenham Court Road. We made a tremendous success there. Wherever we went, we made a success. And then, on that, he bought a great big place, which was an airplane factory, back in Hammersmith. He signed us up to a six-month contract, with the stipulation that he could put us into another place. And they go to work and remodel this place called the Palli de Dades Hammersmith. And they put us in Hammersmith. Hammersmith's a place, I'd say it was half a block, like you, this way, and almost a square level, 300 feet long, and about 150 feet wide. Now, we have no equipment to help us out. We've grown for playing our instruments, and we feel that harm, that harm. After the week, I jumped there. Robinson, while I was at Rectors, his wife became sick, and he had to return to the United States. He couldn't stand the weather. In his way, Billy Jones, an English pianist, gets into the Dixieland jazz band. Now, here to Florida, I've only went to New Orleans for two different men. Now, this is an Englishman who had heard these recordings, dialed himself on the records, and he played opposite of us in Rectors. And I tried him out for the job, rehearsed it, and he did a good job because some of the records in the English make records, he has played on them, and you'll be able to hear them because if the Tulane gets the records and made it in England, Billy Jones will be on there, and you'll hear he's playing just as good as any American man played because he was styled on the records. In the rhythm. Now, Jones and we played there six months, and after that, he gave us almost another six-month contact, and I didn't renew no more because the pound was falling. He was down to 442, and I didn't want to change the money into American money, and we decided to come back to the United States. Christian came along with me, and when we got back, the war had stopped. Edwards was demobilized out of the Army and had a little band of his own. I don't know what he called his band, but they weren't doing nothing, so I asked you this, you want your place in the band? Because whenever anybody was in the band, they stayed in the band. Like when Edwards was at Rizuela, he was in the Army. I gave him $50 a week out of the money that was collected out of the collection box to help him out. When Ragus was sick, I did the same thing to her. You'll see many numbers in it. When he was in the Army, and Miss Ragus' husband had died, that they're still derived rather to it, for my generosity, of giving them a share and a cut on the records was going to follow. Yet, these people put me down as a thief. When you read Miss Ragus' mail, you'll know different. I took care of them, all of them. I was the only man that knew anything about business in the band. I'd come up the hard way. I only knew one thing, I had to make a success. When we went to Paladin Dance, we played a few sets there. We had 5,800 people on the opening night. So I started playing some English numbers that they knew over there, like, I can't think of the numbers now, was Cole Porter's number. I never realized, da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Oh, they liked that kind of stuff. And then many others, like, I got my captain working for me now in different popular tunes, and every now and then I'd slap them one of these snot balls that I had. You understand? That's all I call them, but today they classed me as a great composer. I've looked upon myself as nobody. Just a man was a figure, put these things together. And I was before the rest of them, and they followed me. we played there, we made a huge success. And if you'll see in there, when...
The man offered me jobs to come back. I had jobs for Paris. And I came back to New York in 1920. I left English piano player. Can we stop now? Yeah.
